title: Hadith
def: A report of the sayings, actions or approvals of the Prophet Muhammad.
what: Each hadith has two parts: the matn, the text, and the isnād, the chain of people who passed it on. Collectors graded reports by the reliability of the narrators and by whether the text agreed with better-attested reports and with the Quran. The best known collections are Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, with four others, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa’i and Ibn Majah, usually counted with them.
Scholars themselves wrote works listing fabricated reports, and graded many as weak or false.
misread: That hadith are late forgeries, and all of them are treated as equally binding.
sources: Bukhari is traditionally said to have chosen roughly seven thousand reports, counting repetitions, from several hundred thousand he examined. The criticism that some reports are weak is one Muslim scholars made first, in their own books. For the Muslim, the issue is not whether a report exists but how well it is attested.

title: Hafsa
def: A wife of the Prophet, daughter of Umar, who kept the first written collection of the Quran.
what: Hafsa bint Umar married the Prophet after her first husband died at Badr. After the collection of the Quran’s leaves under Abu Bakr, the copy was kept in her care, and Uthman later borrowed it to make the standard copies, then returned it (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: Hair
def: The Prophet’s hair was kept by some Companions as a keepsake; Muslims differ on the practice, and the Prophet wore his hair in the manner of his time.
what: Anas related that the barber shaved the Prophet’s head at the Farewell Pilgrimage and that the Companions took his hair, each a hair or two (Sahih Muslim). Umm Salama kept some of it in a vessel (Sahih al-Bukhari). The Prophet is reported to have first let his hair fall like the People of the Book, and later parted it (Sahih al-Bukhari).
sources: Some scholars permit seeking blessing from the Prophet’s relics, and others, particularly Salafis, discourage it so as not to lead to veneration. The hair at the Hajj is shaved or cut as a sign of the end of the state of ihram.

title: Haj Amin al-Husseini and the Handschar
def: A Palestinian leader who collaborated with the Nazis; the SS Handschar division was a small part of the Muslims who fought in the war.
what: Haj Amin al-Husseini (1895–1974) was Mufti of Jerusalem, a Palestinian nationalist opposed to Zionism, who lived in Germany during the war and helped to recruit Bosnian Muslims for the 13th Waffen-SS “Handschar” division in 1943. The division’s record included mutiny and desertion by many of its soldiers.
misread: That the Muslim world was allied with the Nazis.
sources: Millions of Muslims fought for the Allies, in the British Indian Army, the Red Army and the Free French forces; tens of thousands of Bosnian Muslims joined the Partisans. Albanian Muslims sheltered Jews on the principle of besa, a pledge of honour, and Muslim families in Bosnia hid Jews, among them the one who kept the Sarajevo Haggadah. The mufti’s collaboration is condemned by most Muslims as an act of a political leader and not a duty of the faith.

title: Hajar
def: Hagar, mother of Ishmael, whose search for water for her son is remembered in the rite of Safa and Marwa.
what: Ibn Abbas relates in Sahih al-Bukhari that Hagar, an Egyptian given to Sarah, was left with her infant son in the barren valley of Mecca. She ran seven times between Safa and Marwa in search of help, until Gabriel struck the ground and the spring of Zamzam came forth. Pilgrims repeat her search in the saʿy.
sources: Where the Bible describes her expulsion (Genesis 21), the Muslim tradition has her settled by Abraham on God’s command. The Prophet said, “may God have mercy on the mother of Ishmael; if she had left Zamzam alone, it would be a flowing spring” (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: Hajar al-Aswad
def: The Black Stone set in the corner of the Kaaba, which pilgrims touch or salute in the circling.
what: The stone is set in the south-east corner of the Kaaba. Umar, kissing it, is reported to have said: “I know that you are only a stone that can neither harm nor benefit; if I had not seen the Prophet kiss you, I would not have kissed you” (Sahih al-Bukhari). Before the Prophet’s mission, according to Ibn Ishaq, the Quraysh disputed who should put it back when the Kaaba was rebuilt, and he laid it on a cloak so that each clan could lift a corner.
misread: That kissing the Black Stone is idol worship.
sources: Muslims do not pray to the stone, and do not have to touch it; the circling can be done by pointing a hand at it from afar. The practice is one of following the Prophet, and Umar’s words state it.

title: Hajj
def: The pilgrimage to Mecca, required once in a lifetime of every Muslim who is able, and the fifth pillar.
what: “Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by people who are able to undertake it” (3:97). Pilgrims enter a state of iḥrām, wearing two plain sheets, circle the Kaaba (ṭawāf), walk between Safa and Marwa, stand at Arafat on the ninth of Dhu al-Hijja, spend the night at Muzdalifa, throw stones at the pillars at Mina, offer an animal (hadī), shave or cut the hair (ḥalq), and make a farewell circling. Those who join the pilgrimage to the lesser pilgrimage in the same trip perform tamattuʿ.
misread: That the rites are pagan, adopted from the idol-worshippers of Mecca.
sources: Muslims hold that the rites were set by Abraham, who built the House (2:125–127; 22:26–29), and that the pagan Arabs corrupted them. The Quran corrects the practices: “pour forth from where the people pour forth” (2:199), and there is to be no quarrel in the Hajj (2:197). Non-Muslims may not enter the sacred area of Mecca (9:28). The sacrificial animal is meant for the poor, the Quran says, and “neither its meat nor its blood reaches God, but piety reaches Him” (22:37). Before the Prophet’s mission, Zayd ibn Amr, a monotheist of Mecca, was reported to have refused food offered to idols, and the Prophet is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari to have declined meat sacrificed to idols.

title: Halal and haram food
def: The Quran forbids carrion, blood, pork and meat over which a name other than God’s was invoked, and permits the rest.
what: “He has forbidden you only carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than God has been invoked; but whoever is compelled, without desire or transgression, there is no sin on him” (2:173, 5:3, 6:145, 16:115). The food of the People of the Book is lawful for Muslims, and theirs for Muslims (5:5). Alcohol is forbidden (5:90). The Quran also says, “eat of the good things, and do good” (23:51).
sources: The reasons given are obedience and the care of body and soul, and the Quran is silent about medical explanations. The permission under necessity is broad: a Muslim who has no other food may eat what is forbidden.

title: Halekon
def: A custom in parts of Afghanistan in which powerful men keep boys for sexual use; it is forbidden in Islam and condemned by Muslim scholars.
what: The practice, known as bacha bazi (“boy play”), is a tribal custom of exploitation and abuse of boys by older men, which has persisted in some areas of Afghanistan and Central Asia. It is not an Islamic practice. The Quran condemns the acts of the people of Lot (7:80–84, 27:54–55), and Islamic law forbids sexual relations outside marriage.
sources: The Taliban banned it in the 1990s and it persisted among warlords after their fall; the Afghan government has made it a crime. Muslim scholars condemn it as abuse and fornication.

title: Haman
def: Pharaoh’s minister in the Quran, whom Pharaoh tells to build a tower (28:38).
what: The Quran names Haman as one of Pharaoh’s men (28:6, 28:8, 28:38, 29:39, 40:24, 40:36). Pharaoh says: “Haman, light a fire for me upon the clay and build me a lofty tower, that I may look up to the God of Moses” (28:38).
misread: That the Quran confuses the Persian Haman of the Book of Esther with an official of Egypt.
sources: The Quran says only that he was an official in Pharaoh’s court, and does not connect him with Esther’s story, in which he is a Persian vizier a thousand years later. The name Hmn is found in Egyptian: the falcon god Hemen was worshipped in Egypt, and compound names were formed with it. Muslim writers have argued from this, and scholars still debate it. The two figures share a name and little else.

title: Hamza
def: The Prophet’s uncle and foster-brother, called “the Lion of God”, killed at Uhud in 625.
what: Hamza accepted Islam in the second year after the Prophet’s call, after he struck Abu Jahl for insulting him, and was among the strongest of the Muslims. He fought at Badr, and was killed at Uhud by Wahshi, a slave of the Quraysh, and his body was mutilated. The Prophet is said to have wept for him, and called him “the master of the martyrs”.

title: Hanif
def: An upright monotheist who is neither Jew nor Christian: the Quran’s word for Abraham’s faith (3:67).
what: “Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists” (3:67). In Arabia before Islam, the ḥunafāʾ were monotheists who rejected the idols without belonging to a religious group, among them Zayd ibn Amr and Waraqa ibn Nawfal. Some scholars derive the word from a Syriac word meaning “pagan”, and others from the Arabic ḥanafa, “to incline”.

title: Haqq
def: “The Truth” and “the right”: one of God’s names, and the word for a due.
what: Al-Ḥaqq is among the names of God (22:6, 24:25). The Quran says: “the truth has come and falsehood has vanished; falsehood is bound to vanish” (17:81). Ḥaqq also means a right or due: the rights of God, of people, of the wife and of the neighbour. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari lists rights that the body, the eyes and the family have upon a person.

title: Harpur, Tom
def: A Canadian religious journalist and author whose books argue against traditional Christianity; some Muslim writers cite him.
what: Tom Harpur wrote on Christian origins, claiming that the Gospel story is a retelling of older myths. Mainstream historians and theologians, Christian and non-Christian, reject this. Some Muslim writers quote him, and Muslims who rely on him accept a view that the Quran does not teach: that Jesus did not exist.

title: Harut and Marut
def: Two figures named in the Quran as teaching magic at Babylon as a test (2:102); Muslim scholars reject the later story that they were fallen angels.
what: The Quran says that the devils taught people magic, and “what was sent down on the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. They did not teach anyone without saying: ‘We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve’” (2:102). Some read “two angels” and others “two kings”, by a variant in the vowel.
sources: Later commentary tells of angels who fell in love with a woman, the planet Venus, and were punished. Ibn Kathir and Qadi Iyad, and most scholars, class the story as an isrāʾīlī tale with no sound chain, which cannot stand against the Quran’s own statement that angels do not disobey (66:6). The verse says only that the two were a test, and that magic is disbelief.

title: Hasan ibn Ali
def: The Prophet’s elder grandson (625–670), who made peace with Muawiya to end the civil war.
what: Hasan, son of Ali and Fatima, was the Prophet’s grandson. The Prophet said of him “this son of mine is a master; God will make peace between two great groups of Muslims through him” (Sahih al-Bukhari). He became caliph after Ali’s death in 661 and gave up the office to Muawiya within months, to end the fighting. He died in 670, reportedly poisoned.
aliases: Hasan B. Ali. B. Abi Talib

title: Hassan ibn Thabit
def: The Prophet’s poet, who answered the satires of the Quraysh in verse.
what: Hassan ibn Thabit of Medina, a Khazraji, was known as the poet of the Prophet. The Prophet set a pulpit for him in the mosque and said: “O Hassan, answer for the Messenger of God; O God, support him with the Holy Spirit” (Sahih al-Bukhari). He wrote elegies for the dead of Uhud and Hamza.
sources: The pre-Islamic poetry tradition was a forum for argument, and Hassan’s verse was answered in kind. The Prophet’s response to poets who mocked him varied from patience to a general amnesty at the conquest of Mecca.

title: Hatred and hate speech
def: The Quran forbids letting hatred of a people make one unjust, and tells Muslims to be kind to those who do not fight them.
what: “Do not let hatred of a people prevent you from being just; be just, that is closer to piety” (5:8). “God does not forbid you from being kind and fair to those who have not fought you over religion” (60:8). The Prophet said: “Do not hate one another, do not envy one another” (Sahih al-Bukhari).
misread: That Muslims are taught to hate non-Muslims.
sources: Some scholars teach a strong form of the doctrine of al-walāʾ wa-l-barāʾ, loyalty to Muslims and disavowal of unbelievers, and others limit it to disavowal of unbelief itself and not of people. Muslims are among the victims of hate crime in many countries, and many Muslim organisations support laws against incitement. Where speech about religion is concerned, the Quran says to answer arguments by arguments, in the way that is best (16:125).

title: Hawariyyun
def: The disciples of Jesus, whom the Quran calls the helpers of God, who said “we are Muslims” (3:52).
what: “When Jesus sensed disbelief from them he said: ‘Who are my helpers toward God?’ The disciples said: ‘We are God’s helpers; we believe in God, and bear witness that we are Muslims (submitters)’” (3:52). The Quran does not give their number or names. “Muslim” here means those who submit to God.
misread: That Muslims claim Paul corrupted the message of Jesus.
sources: Some Muslim writers say Paul changed Jesus’ teaching, a view not found in the Quran or the hadith. Others hold that the disciples’ message was kept in part and distorted over time. Historians date Paul’s letters to before the Gospels. The Quran’s own claim is about what Jesus taught: the worship of one God.

title: Hazrat
def: A title of respect, mostly in South Asia, for men of high standing in the religion.
what: Ḥaḍrat (“presence”) is used before the names of prophets, Companions and respected scholars and saints, as in “Hazrat Ali”. It is not a rank conferred by any authority, and has no resemblance to the formal canonisation of saints in the Catholic Church.

title: Hell
def: The Quran describes Hell in vivid terms as a punishment for those who reject truth and do wrong; scholars hold that God is just and merciful in it.
what: The Quran speaks of Hell’s fire, boiling water and the tree of Zaqqum (44:43–46, 56:52–54), and warns of it often, so that it may be avoided. It also says: “We never punish until We have sent a messenger” (17:15), and that God “does not wrong anyone, even by an atom’s weight” (4:40).
misread: That Islam is preoccupied with torment, and that no one can escape it.
sources: The Quran describes the same God as “the Most Merciful of those who show mercy”. The Prophet said that God’s mercy outstrips His wrath (Sahih al-Bukhari). Hadith of intercession say that those with even an atom of faith will in the end be brought out (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim). Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim are reported to have held that Hell will end, a view other scholars reject, which shows that Muslims have differed on this.

title: Heraclius
def: The Byzantine emperor (610–641), who according to Muslim sources received a letter from the Prophet inviting him to Islam.
what: Sahih al-Bukhari (the seventh hadith) relates that Heraclius, receiving the letter, sent for Arab traders in his territory. He asked Abu Sufyan, then still an enemy of the Prophet, about his family, his followers, his honesty and his teaching. Heraclius said that if what Abu Sufyan said was true, “he will rule the ground beneath my feet”. He did not accept Islam. The Byzantine and Armenian sources have little on this meeting.

title: Hijab
def: Modest dress, and in particular the head covering worn by many Muslim women.
what: In the Quran ḥijāb means a screen or barrier, as in the verse about speaking to the Prophet’s wives from behind a screen (33:53). The covering of the head and chest is described by other words: khimār (24:31) and jilbāb (33:59). Scholars agree that modest dress is required of men and of women, and they differ on the details, including the face.
misread: That the hijab is a sign of oppression imposed on Muslim women.
sources: The Quran says that there is “no compulsion in religion” (2:256), and many Muslim scholars hold that forcing a woman to veil, as some states do, has no basis in the sources. Many Muslim women who wear it describe it as their own choice and an expression of faith, and many others do not wear it. The issue for the Muslim is consent: being made to veil and being forbidden to veil are both an infringement.

title: Hijra
def: Emigration for the sake of faith, above all the Prophet’s move from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.
what: After thirteen years of persecution in Mecca, the Prophet and his followers left for Medina in 622 CE. Under Umar the Islamic calendar was counted from this year. Hijra also means leaving what God forbids, as in the hadith “the emigrant is the one who abandons what God has forbidden” (Sahih al-Bukhari).
An earlier emigration, around 615, took a group of Muslims across the Red Sea to Abyssinia, where a Christian king, the Negus, gave them refuge.
misread: That the move was the start of a policy of conquest.
sources: Ibn Ishaq relates that Ja’far ibn Abi Talib recited from chapter 19, on Mary, before the Negus, who wept and said that this and what Jesus brought came from the same lamp. The first Muslims were refugees from persecution who were sheltered by a Christian ruler. Medina’s early constitution, preserved in Ibn Ishaq’s biography, treats the Jews of the city as a community alongside the Muslims.

title: Hijri calendar
def: The Islamic lunar calendar, counted from the Prophet’s migration to Medina in 622.
what: It has twelve lunar months of 29 or 30 days, a year of about 354 days, so its months move through the seasons: Ramadan falls about eleven days earlier each solar year. Umar fixed the era from the hijra in 638 (17 AH). The Quran says that “the number of months with God is twelve” (9:36), and condemns postponing months (nasīʾ) as “an increase in disbelief” (9:37).
sources: The month of Dhu al-Qida is one of the four sacred months of truce, and Dhu al-Hijja the month of pilgrimage. The Quran’s ban on adding a month to line the calendar up with the sun explains why Ramadan moves through the year.

title: Historicity of the early sources
def: How scholars date and test the sources for Islam’s beginnings: the Quran, the biographies, the hadith, and outside witnesses.
what: Muslims trace the sources by chains of narrators, as in the entries on isnad and sira. Non-Muslim historians also use inscriptions, coins, papyri and writers of the time. Christian texts from the 630s–660s mention an Arab prophet and the conquests, among them the Doctrina Jacobi (c. 634), Thomas the Presbyter (c. 640) and Sebeos (660s). Early Islamic coins and the Dome of the Rock inscriptions date from the 690s.
sources: Key dates in Muslim tradition: Muhammad’s birth about 570; the first revelation about 610; the hijra 622; Badr 624; the Trench 627; Hudaybiyya 628; the conquest of Mecca 630; his death 632; the four rightly guided caliphs to 661; the Umayyads to 750; the Abbasids to 1258. Historians differ on how far the later biographies can be trusted for detail, some holding them reliable in outline and others sceptical, and Muslim scholars apply their own tests.

title: Hitler, Adolf
def: A name that comes up in polemics between Muslims and Christians; Islam judges deeds and not labels.
what: Arguments about whether Hitler was a Christian, or about his relations with the Church, are a Christian-Muslim polemical topic, and not a matter of Islamic teaching. His regime murdered six million Jews and millions of others, in an act which Muslim scholars condemn by the standard of the Quran: “whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all of mankind” (5:32).

title: Hitta
def: The word the Israelites were told to say on entering the city, meaning “relief” or “forgiveness” (2:58, 7:161).
what: “Enter the gate prostrating, and say ‘hiṭṭa’, and We will forgive you your sins” (2:58). The Quran says that those who changed the word to another were punished (2:59). Commentators relate that they entered crawling on their backs and said “a grain in a hair” in mockery.

title: Homosexuality
def: Islamic tradition forbids same-sex acts, from the story of Lot’s people; scholars have differed about the penalty and Muslim societies about how to treat people.
what: The Quran tells of Lot’s people, who “approach men in lust instead of women” and were destroyed (7:80–84, 26:165–166, 27:54–55). The act is called an indecency (fāḥisha). The Quran sets no worldly penalty. Classical jurists differed, and the Hanafis did not prescribe the fixed punishment for it, while others held that it was the same as for adultery, or death. A report on killing both partners (Abu Dawud) is graded weak by many.
misread: That Islam teaches that people may be killed for their orientation.
sources: The tradition draws a line between acts and inclinations, and the standard of proof (four witnesses, as for adultery) is so high that the penalty is almost never applicable. The Prophet forbade spying on people’s private lives (49:12). Muslim societies today differ widely: some criminalise, some tolerate quietly, and a minority of Muslim scholars and writers argue for a different reading. Violence and vigilantism against people have no basis in Islamic law.

title: Honorifics
def: The blessings Muslims add after the name of a prophet: “peace be upon him” (A.S., PBUH, ﷺ).
what: “God and His angels send blessings on the Prophet; O you who believe, send blessings on him and greet him with peace” (33:56). Muslims say it after the Prophet’s name (ṣallā Allāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallam), and “peace be upon him” (ʿalayhi al-salām) after other prophets. For Companions the phrase is raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu, “may God be pleased with him”.

title: Houris
def: The “wide-eyed” companions promised in Paradise; the Quran also promises pure spouses to all believers.
what: The Quran describes “ḥūr ʿīn” (44:54, 52:20, 56:22), companions of modest gaze whom no man or jinn has touched (55:56). It also promises “pure spouses” to all who believe (2:25, 3:15, 4:57) and says that the believers will enter Paradise “and their wives” (36:56, 43:70). The number seventy-two does not appear in the Quran, but in a single report in al-Tirmidhi.
misread: That a suicide attacker earns seventy-two virgins.
sources: Muslim scholars have said that the texts apply to all believers, men and women, whom God will join with spouses suited to them, and that the images of the afterlife are described in terms familiar to people. The Prophet said that suicide leads to Hell. Scholars have broadly condemned the use of the idea as a reward for violence. A theory that the word means “white grapes” in Syriac is not accepted by most scholars.

title: Houses and homes
def: The Quran calls the home a place of rest (16:80) and tells believers to ask permission before entering another’s house (24:27).
what: “God has made your homes a place of rest for you” (16:80). “O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own until you have asked permission and greeted their people” (24:27). “If you do not find anyone in it, do not enter until permission is given you; and if you are told to go back, then go back” (24:28).

title: Hud
def: The prophet sent to the people of ʿĀd (7:65–72, 11:50–60), who rejected him.
what: Hud told his people to worship God alone, and said he asked no reward for it (11:50–51). They called him foolish and said that their gods had afflicted him (11:53–54). He answered: “I put my trust in God, my Lord and your Lord; there is no creature but He holds it by its forelock” (11:56). A violent wind destroyed them (69:6–8). Chapter 11 is named after him.

title: Hudaybiyya
def: A treaty of 628 between the Prophet and Quraysh, which the Quran calls “a clear victory” (48:1).
what: In 628 the Prophet set out with about 1,400 men for the lesser pilgrimage, and was stopped at al-Hudaybiya outside Mecca. The Muslims pledged allegiance under a tree (48:18). The treaty provided for a ten-year truce, a return of the Prophet and the Muslims the next year to perform the pilgrimage, and that Quraysh men who joined Muhammad without permission be returned. At the signing, the Quraysh envoy objected to “Muhammad, messenger of God” and the Prophet agreed to write “son of Abdullah”.
sources: Many of the Companions were distressed at the terms. The Quran, revealed on the way back, called it a clear victory (48:1), and the truce allowed the Muslims to spread their message freely, so that two years later Mecca opened to them without a battle.

title: Hudud
def: The fixed punishments of Islamic law for a small number of offences, hedged with strict conditions.
what: The word means “limits”. The offences are theft, highway robbery, adultery, false accusation of adultery and, for some jurists, drinking and apostasy. The Prophet said: “Avoid the hudud wherever you can” (al-Tirmidhi, in other versions “avert”). Proof is demanding, any doubt prevents them, and repentance can remove them.
sources: Umar suspended the penalty for theft during a famine. Many modern scholars hold the hudud are rarely applicable without conditions that are hard to meet.

title: Hui
def: A Chinese people who are Muslim and make up about half of China’s Muslims.
what: The Hui, who number over ten million, are Chinese in language and culture and Muslim in religion, and live in every province, most densely in Ningxia and Gansu. They descend from Arab and Persian traders and from Chinese converts. The Great Mosque of Xi’an, in a Chinese temple style, is one of the oldest, from the eighth century.

title: Hukm
def: Judgement or rule: the Quran says that judgement belongs to God (12:40), and the word is also used for a ruling in law.
what: “Judgement belongs only to God” (12:40, 6:57). The Kharijites used the words “no judgement but God’s” against Ali, who said that it was “a true word by which a falsehood is meant”. In law, ḥukm is the status of an act, one of five: obligatory, recommended, permitted, disliked or forbidden.

title: Human dignity
def: The Quran says God has honoured the children of Adam (17:70) and that all are of one origin (4:1, 49:13).
what: “We have honoured the children of Adam, and carried them on land and sea” (17:70). “O mankind, fear your Lord who created you from a single soul” (4:1). The Farewell Sermon states the sanctity of life, property and honour, and that all are descended from Adam. Muslim scholars have drawn on these texts in forming statements of human rights, for example the 1990 Cairo Declaration and the 1981 Universal Islamic Declaration.

title: Hunayn
def: A battle in 630 in a valley near Mecca, where the Muslims were first routed and then won.
what: After the conquest of Mecca the Prophet fought the tribes of Hawazin and Thaqif at Hunayn. The Muslims, who were many, trusted in their numbers and were at first scattered. The Quran recalls: “on the day of Hunayn, when your great numbers pleased you but availed you nothing” (9:25), and “then God sent down His tranquillity on His Messenger” (9:26). The Muslims rallied and won.
sources: After the battle the Prophet released the captives of Hawazin on their request and gave gifts to Meccan leaders to win their hearts, which angered some of the Ansar until he spoke to them (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: Hunayn ibn Ishaq
def: A Nestorian Christian physician (809–873) who led the translation of Greek works into Arabic for the Abbasid court.
what: Hunayn ibn Ishaq of al-Hira studied medicine in Baghdad and learned Greek. He and his school translated many of the works of Galen and Hippocrates, Plato and Aristotle, and the Greek Old Testament, and he wrote on eye diseases. He is called “the sheikh of the translators”. He was a Christian working for Muslim caliphs.

title: Hunting
def: The Quran allows hunting with trained animals (5:4) but forbids it to pilgrims in the state of ihram (5:94–96).
what: “They ask you what is lawful for them. Say: the good things, and what you have taught your trained hunting animals, training them as God taught you; eat of what they catch for you, and mention God’s name over it” (5:4). “Do not kill game while you are in ihram” (5:95).

title: Husayn ibn Ali
def: The Prophet’s younger grandson (626–680), killed at Karbala, whose death Muslims regard as a great crime.
what: Husayn, son of Ali and Fatima, was loved by the Prophet, who called him and Hasan “the masters of the youth of Paradise” (al-Tirmidhi). After Muawiya’s death in 680 he refused to give allegiance to Yazid and was killed with his small band at Karbala on the tenth of Muharram, 61 AH.
sources: Ashura is also the day on which, by a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, Moses was saved from Pharaoh, and the Prophet encouraged fasting on it.
aliases: Husain B. Ali. B. Abi Talib

title: Hypocrites
def: Those who profess faith but do not believe, whom the Quran warns against in chapter 63 and elsewhere.
what: The Quran says that “when the hypocrites come to you they say: ‘we bear witness that you are the Messenger of God’… and God bears witness that the hypocrites are liars” (63:1), and that they are “in the lowest depth of the Fire” (4:145). The Prophet said: “The signs of a hypocrite are three: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is trusted he betrays” (Sahih al-Bukhari).
sources: The Prophet did not execute the hypocrites of Medina, among them Abdullah ibn Ubayy, though their identity was known, and said that people would say Muhammad kills his companions. The judgement on what is in people’s hearts is left to God.
